blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Spatial representation is one of the most fundamental capacities of
biological perception. Humans and other animals do not experience the world
as a sequence of independent retinal images. Through continuous exploration,
they maintain information about the surrounding space, keep track of objects
that are no longer visible, update their own location as they move, and use
this information to guide subsequent behavior. These abilities are not
inherently linguistic: they arise from perception and from sensorimotor
interaction with the environment.

blocks.en:
Several classical ideas in perception and spatial cognition point to this
view. Object-file theories describe how object-specific information remains
associated with the same entity across changes in its visual appearance [ 17 ] . Spatial updating and path integration describe how
an internal estimate of location is continuously revised from self-motion [ 26 ] . Sensorimotor contingency theories further emphasize
that perception involves knowledge of how sensory input would change under
possible actions [ 30 ] . Together, these perspectives suggest
that a useful representation of space should describe more than what is
visible in the current image: it should maintain a state of the surrounding
world that persists and evolves as the observer interacts with it.

environments; object dynamics, contact physics, and complete physical world
modeling are outside it.

blocks.en: 5 Related Work
blocks.zh: 5 相关工作

blocks.en:
Frozen-feature probing asks what information is already accessible in a
representation without updating the backbone. Self-supervised image
encoders such as DINO and DINOv2 revealed that semantic organization,
object boundaries, and strong local correspondences emerge without dense
labels [ 6 , 29 ] . More recent work extends
this methodology to video foundation models: VidFM3D evaluates whether
shallow readouts recover depth, camera pose, and 3D point structure from
frozen video-model features, and analyzes how these signals vary with
network depth and diffusion timestep [ 15 ] . Related
probes of image foundation models test depth, surface normals, and
multi-view correspondence [ 11 ] , scene-level tasks
such as 3D question answering, visual grounding, and registration [ 25 ] , and novel-view synthesis from features read out
as 3D Gaussians [ 9 ] . Feed-forward 3D reconstruction
models, from DUSt3R to VGGT and Fast3R, provide a geometry-specialized
reference point because their training directly targets multi-view
reconstruction and camera estimation [ 37 , 35 , 38 ] ; streaming variants
such as Spann3R and CUT3R carry an explicit spatial memory or a persistent
state that is updated with every new frame [ 34 , 36 ] . Our streaming prefixes ask a
related question of general-purpose representations without assuming such
a state. Our work
starts from the same evidence-first principle but changes the object of
evaluation: metric geometry is one functional diagnostic rather than a
definition of spatial state, and we also ask whether a representation
supports view consistency, object persistence, predictive spatial update,
and actionability. Two models with similar depth readout can therefore
receive very different spatial-state profiles, and strong future-feature
retrieval is not credited as predictive spatial update unless it passes
matched motion controls.

blocks.en:
Large video generators such as Wan and CogVideoX are optimized for
denoising and visual synthesis rather than for downstream readout [ 33 , 41 ] . Nevertheless, work on image
diffusion models has shown that semantic and geometric consistency can be
extracted from internal activations, and that useful information is
distributed across both network layers and diffusion timesteps [ 31 , 23 ] . Recent probing of
video diffusion transformers similarly reports that physical and
3D-related signals are most accessible at intermediate blocks and
nontrivial noise levels [ 15 , 12 ] .
This motivates our layer × \times generation-coordinate × \times streaming-prefix analysis: we compare selected extraction settings rather
than assuming that one hidden state characterizes an entire model. Such
profiles describe accessibility during computation, not when a capability
emerges during training.

Spatial ability is often evaluated through language. SpatialVLM and
SpatialRGPT improve quantitative and region-level spatial question
answering by training vision-language models on large synthetic spatial
data [ 7 , 10 ] , and VSI-Bench asks
multimodal LLMs to remember and recall the layout of a space from video,
finding that generating cognitive maps improves distance estimates [ 39 ] . Cambrian-S argues that such training
alone does not yield robust implicit spatial representations and proposes
predictive sensing, in which latent next-frame prediction decides what to
remember [ 40 ] . A growing set of studies probes the
representations themselves. SeeSE3 finds subspaces of self-supervised
vision features that align with 3D Euclidean space, with camera motion
linearly accessible from feature displacements [ 8 ] ;
SpaRRTa shows that visual foundation models differ markedly in how well
they encode the relative positions of objects [ 19 ] ;
probes of V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAE-v2 decode camera motion best at 60–70%
of network depth while intuitive physics stays near chance [ 28 ] , and in video encoders, motion direction
becomes decodable only within an intermediate-depth zone [ 16 ] . For multimodal LLMs, the spatial benefit of
a visual representation tracks its 3D structure, measured by the
cross-view consistency of latent features or the accuracy of explicit
geometry [ 14 ] . Our study complements these probes by reading
several functional levels of spatial state, including object persistence,
predictive update, and goal use, from the same ten representations under
matched controls.

physical regularities remains contested: diffusion models trained on

learning across many simulated tasks [ 45 ] . Our L3 and L4

updates and goal-conditioned actions can be read out from the represented
state.

blocks.en:
Object-centric learning explicitly decomposes scenes into entity-level
latent variables. Slot Attention learns exchangeable slots that bind to
objects, and sequential extensions such as SAVi propagate and correct
object slots through video [ 21 , 20 ] .
These approaches build an object-centric format into the architecture,
whereas the foundation models we evaluate generally use distributed patch
or video tokens, and we do not assume that their internal state is
slot-based. Our question is operational: can an object’s bearing be
recovered after it is no longer visible? This differs from
violation-of-expectation benchmarks such as IntPhys 2, which assess the
discrimination of possible from impossible events involving permanence,
continuity, solidity, or immutability [ 4 ] ; V-JEPA
surprise scores perform well on several such conditions [ 13 ] , but plausibility discrimination does
not measure object persistence directly. In generated video, current world
models usually resume a target that comes back into view in the state it
was left in, rather than letting its event progress while it was unseen [ 22 ] . We therefore predict an explicit
bearing in the current camera frame and use history interventions to test
which visual evidence supports that readout.

blocks.en: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6. 讨论和结论

blocks.en:
We characterized spatial state representations through four functional
levels: spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update,
and actionability. Across ten frozen representations, no model leads on
every task, and the readouts vary with the extraction layer and the
streaming prefix. The levels are linked by two ingredient chains:
camera-pose readout supports object persistence, which in turn supports
goal-conditioned action, whereas feature prediction builds on
visible-scene readout and is unrelated to persistence. Matched controls
show that decodability, input use, and functional utility dissociate: a
probe can localize accurately without using history, a natively predicted
feature retains recoverable structure but not the original readout
interface, and a goal-sensitive action readout need not benefit from the
correct goal. Together, these results support multidimensional evaluation
of spatial state beyond a single task score. Our conclusions concern
frozen feature interfaces, trained probes, and offline indoor
trajectories: independently encoded causal prefixes characterize what a
representation of the observed history affords rather than an incremental
state update, and retrieval scores in different target feature spaces do
not share a physical error scale.
